reviewPolicy: Every question received an independent second-pass review for one-best-answer validity, distractor quality, explanation binding, semantic drift, and rights safety before acceptance.

questions.prompt: What should a reviewer identify first when a Python value crosses into a security-sensitive operation?
options: The framework version only
Who controls the value, what validates it, and which interpreter or sink receives it
Whether the function is short
Whether the browser rendered the form
questions.explanation: Control, validation, and interpretation establish the trust boundary; code size and browser rendering do not establish server authority.

review.note: Single best answer; distractors do not describe a trust boundary.

questions.prompt: When is Source / Validation / Sink most useful in a secure-code review?
options: When every security decision can be reduced to a regular expression
When only UI behavior is being inspected
When a concrete value can be traced from an untrusted source through a control to an interpreting sink
When the generated code is accepted without tests
questions.explanation: The framework clarifies a concrete data flow. It does not replace authorization, provenance, or human review.

review.note: Framework scope is explicit and the explanation preserves its limits.

questions.prompt: Which request is the strongest starting prompt for generating a secure Python handler?
options: Write the shortest handler possible
Make it production-ready and trust all validated-looking input
Copy a familiar implementation and omit edge cases
State the requirements, trust assumptions, allowed inputs, failure behavior, and tests before requesting code
questions.explanation: A bounded prompt makes security assumptions and acceptance criteria reviewable before generated code is considered.

review.note: Correct option tests prompt completeness, not a particular vendor or tool.

questions.prompt: What is the security authority of AI-generated Python before human review?
options: An untrusted draft that requires source review, tests, and human acceptance
An automatically approved implementation
A grading oracle
A substitute for the requirements
questions.explanation: Generated output is an input to review. It cannot independently authorize a security decision, grade, or release.

review.note: Authority boundary is unambiguous and aligned to the curriculum scope.

questions.prompt: Which record best supports human re-verification of an AI repair?
options: The model name alone
The original requirement, generated revision, tests, reviewer decision, and residual-risk note
A screenshot of the prompt only
The fact that the code compiled
questions.explanation: Re-verification needs traceable context and evidence, not a model label or compilation result alone.

review.note: Evidence requirements are concrete without implementing an Evidence system.

questions.prompt: Which validation design is the strongest for a user-selected report name?
options: Remove punctuation until the string looks safe
Accept every non-empty string and rely on downstream code
Define the allowed grammar, type, length, and range, then reject values outside it
Allow the browser to decide which characters are safe
questions.explanation: Validation should implement the feature's explicit grammar and bounds at the server boundary.

review.note: Blacklist and client-trust distractors are plausible but clearly wrong.

questions.prompt: How should an untrusted value normally enter a SQL predicate?
options: By deleting quote characters
By hiding the query from the user
By escaping it with a browser helper
By binding it as a parameter while separately allowlisting any structural identifier
questions.explanation: Parameters preserve SQL structure for values. Table, column, or order identifiers require a closed allowlist because they are not ordinary values.

review.note: The answer distinguishes values from SQL structure.

questions.prompt: Which Python subprocess pattern best reduces command-injection risk?
options: Use a fixed executable, an argument list, shell=False, and an explicit timeout
Join user tokens into a shell command
Pass raw input to a shell because it is quoted later
Let the model choose the executable at runtime
questions.explanation: A fixed executable and argument vector avoid turning untrusted data into shell syntax; timeouts and error handling are additional controls.

review.note: Concrete Python-specific control; no exploit payload is required.

questions.prompt: Why is splitting a command string not the same as safely designing a subprocess call?
options: Splitting always authenticates the caller
It can leave the executable, argument meaning, shell policy, or resource limits uncontrolled
It automatically adds authorization
It makes every program sandboxed
questions.explanation: Tokenization does not by itself establish which program may run, what arguments are allowed, or what resource policy applies.

review.note: Tests the boundary between tokenization and execution policy.

questions.prompt: Why is eval unsuitable for parsing a user-provided expression?
options: It cannot return a value
It only works in Java
It treats input as executable Python rather than constrained data
It automatically applies an allowlist
questions.explanation: eval interprets input as Python code. Use a data format or a narrowly defined parser instead.

review.note: Correctly identifies code injection without conflating it with SQL injection.

questions.prompt: What is the safest default response when generated code proposes exec for configurable behavior?
options: Add a comment and keep exec
Base64-encode the string first
Ask the browser to approve it
Reject the design and replace it with a fixed operation or constrained data model
questions.explanation: Encoding or commenting does not change the execution sink. A fixed operation or constrained parser preserves the intended behavior without executing configuration as code.

review.note: Tests remediation judgment and avoids accepting cosmetic fixes.

questions.prompt: What does parameterization protect in a SQL query?
options: The distinction between SQL structure and a value
The user's authorization decision
The availability of every database table
The correctness of an unrelated file path
questions.explanation: Parameterization protects query structure from value data; authorization and other controls remain separate decisions.

review.note: Scope of the control is stated precisely.

questions.prompt: Why is pickle.loads inappropriate for bytes supplied by an untrusted client?
options: Pickle cannot represent numbers
Unpickling can invoke object construction behavior and is not a safe data parser
Pickle is slower than JSON in every case
It automatically disables file access
questions.explanation: Pickle is a serialization mechanism capable of invoking object behavior during loading; it is not a safe boundary for untrusted bytes.

review.note: Python deserialization risk is accurately bounded.

questions.prompt: Which parser choice is the safer starting point for data-shaped YAML from a request?
options: yaml.load with default object construction
pickle.loads after a filename check
yaml.safe_load followed by schema and size validation
eval on the YAML text
questions.explanation: safe_load reduces object-construction behavior, but schema, size, and business validation are still required.

review.note: Correct answer includes the necessary post-parse validation.

questions.prompt: What must a JSON or YAML parser policy specify before parsed data reaches application logic?
options: Only the file extension
Only the model that generated the request
Only whether parsing raised an exception
Allowed types and fields, size limits, and behavior for unknown or malformed data
questions.explanation: A parser boundary needs an explicit data shape and resource policy; a file extension or model identity is not sufficient.

review.note: No semantic drift from safe-parser objective.

questions.prompt: When could a pickle fixture be a false positive during a code review?
options: When it is read only from an integrity-protected, application-owned test artifact and never from a user-controlled path
Whenever the file ends in .pkl
When a user uploads it through a trusted form
When a prompt says the file is safe
questions.explanation: The risk depends on the actual trust and integrity boundary. Even this exception requires a documented assumption and must not be generalized to user input.

review.note: Explicit false-positive teaching case with assumptions, not blanket approval.

questions.prompt: Which statement about generated code that uses exec is correct?
options: A comment saying 'safe' removes the code-execution sink
It remains a code-execution boundary and needs a fixed-operation redesign or a separately justified trust boundary
It is safe if the input is JSON
It is equivalent to a parameterized SQL query
questions.explanation: The interpreter remains the sink regardless of comments or a superficial input format. The redesign must constrain behavior or prove a narrow, non-user-controlled boundary.

review.note: Reinforces eval/exec distinction from serialization.

questions.prompt: Why should an upload handler avoid using the client filename as its storage path?
options: Client filenames are always empty
A client filename is metadata, not authorization for a filesystem location
File extensions cannot be displayed
Python cannot create directories
questions.explanation: The server should generate storage names and authorize the final location; client metadata can be retained separately if needed.

review.note: Tests file metadata versus server authority.

questions.prompt: What is the important containment check for a user-influenced path?
options: Check that the string contains a dot
Trust a basename without checking the final location
Compare only the raw request text to the base string
Resolve using filesystem-aware rules and verify the final candidate remains under the authorized base
questions.explanation: Lexical checks can disagree with filesystem behavior. Canonical resolution and final-object containment are required, with race and symlink policy where relevant.

review.note: Preserves the distinction between normalization and authorization.

questions.prompt: Which upload policy is the strongest baseline?
options: Generate a server-side name, limit size and content handling, store under an authorized base, and avoid serving active content by default
Trust the extension and serve the original name
Scan only the filename in the browser
Accept unlimited content because storage is private
questions.explanation: Upload security requires storage, content, size, naming, and serving decisions; a client extension is not a security boundary.

review.note: Covers file handling without claiming malware scanning is sufficient.

questions.prompt: Why is checking only that an outbound URL uses https insufficient for SSRF defense?
options: https is never encrypted
The URL may still resolve to an unauthorized host or private address, follow an unsafe redirect, or consume excessive resources
HTTPS automatically disables DNS
The scheme controls authorization
questions.explanation: Outbound policy also needs hostname/IP resolution, redirect, timeout, response-size, and egress controls appropriate to the application.

review.note: SSRF control is multi-layered and Python-agnostic in the correct way.

questions.prompt: What should a reviewer ask about redirects in a server-side fetcher?
options: Whether the browser displays the redirect
Whether the URL was generated by an AI
Whether each redirect is revalidated against the outbound policy or disabled
Whether redirects make authentication unnecessary
questions.explanation: A safe initial URL can redirect to a disallowed destination; the policy must cover the entire request chain.

review.note: Tests a concrete SSRF edge case.

questions.prompt: Which outbound request is a plausible SSRF false positive, assuming the configuration is integrity-protected?
options: requests.get(request.args['url'])
requests.get(url_from_a_user_profile)
requests.get(model_generated_url)
requests.get(a fixed, reviewed service URL with no user-controlled components)
questions.explanation: A fixed reviewed endpoint is not user-controlled network authority under the stated assumption, though timeout, authentication, and egress policy still matter.

review.note: False-positive scope is explicit and does not claim the call is universally safe.

questions.prompt: Where should a reviewer choose output encoding?
options: At the exact output context and sink, such as HTML text, attribute, URL, header, or JSON
Only when the value is first stored
Only at the database boundary
Never, because validation replaces encoding
questions.explanation: Output contexts have different grammars. Encoding or safe serialization must be selected at the actual sink.

review.note: Context-specific output rule is stated without copying certification wording.

questions.prompt: When does a state-changing browser request need a CSRF defense?
options: Only when the request contains JSON
When the browser can attach ambient credentials and an attacker may cause a cross-site request
Never when a user is authenticated
Only when the frontend uses Python
questions.explanation: CSRF concerns ambient credentials and cross-site request initiation. Use a server-verified token, origin policy, or an equivalent defense appropriate to the session design.

review.note: CSRF is explicitly resolved and kept distinct from authentication.

questions.prompt: What should a user-facing Python exception response normally contain?
options: The full traceback and request body
The database connection string
A stable safe message and a correlation reference without secrets or internal details
Whatever message the model generated
questions.explanation: Clients need safe, stable behavior. Operators may need correlated diagnostics, but those must be separately controlled and redacted.

review.note: Separates client and operator channels.

questions.prompt: Why must a log or redirect value be constrained before it is built from request input?
options: To make the stack trace longer
To enable arbitrary response headers
To skip authorization
To prevent control characters or unapproved structure from changing the log or header meaning
questions.explanation: Log and header values have control-character and structural boundaries. Reject or constrain input and use safe structured logging.

review.note: Tests exception/logging and header boundary reasoning.

questions.prompt: Which is a plausible XSS false positive?
options: A value rendered as text by a verified autoescaping template context, with no raw-output bypass
A value inserted into a raw HTML block
A URL assembled from untrusted input without URL policy
A value placed in a script string without JavaScript-safe encoding
questions.explanation: A verified escaped text context can be safe for that sink. The finding must be reopened if the context changes or an escape bypass exists.

review.note: False-positive example is independently authored and context-bounded.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes authentication and authorization?
options: Authentication decides which object a user may edit
Authorization is only a browser display feature
Authentication identifies the subject; authorization decides whether that subject may perform this action on this object
They are interchangeable names for a cookie flag
questions.explanation: Identity and permission are separate server-side decisions, and a successful login does not authorize every object or action.

review.note: Core distinction is clear and not tied to a certification taxonomy.

questions.prompt: What test most directly checks for BOLA/IDOR?
options: Change the page color after login
Use a valid caller identity with another user's valid object identifier and verify the server denies the action
Check only that the endpoint returns JSON
Verify that the client hides the edit button
questions.explanation: BOLA/IDOR is an object-level authorization failure; the server must evaluate the subject, object, action, and policy.

review.note: Test directly targets object substitution and server authority.

questions.prompt: Which session lifecycle event normally warrants identifier rotation?
options: A stylesheet update
A read-only page view
A dependency scan
Login or privilege change
questions.explanation: Rotation at authentication and privilege transitions reduces fixation risk; expiry, revocation, and cookie policy are also required.

review.note: Single best answer and no unrelated implementation claim.

questions.prompt: What should happen when no server-side authorization rule grants an attempted action?
options: Deny by default and avoid revealing unnecessary object existence
Allow it if the client supplied a role
Ask the generated code to choose
Allow reads and deny only deletes
questions.explanation: Default deny prevents an omitted rule from becoming permission. Response uniformity can reduce object enumeration where appropriate.

review.note: Default-deny authority is explicit.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest first question about a sensitive value?
options: How can it be copied into more logs?
Does the system need to collect or return it at all?
Which prompt should contain it?
How can it be hard-coded safely?
questions.explanation: Minimization removes exposure paths before storage, encryption, logging, or access-control complexity is added.

review.note: Tests minimization rather than a particular secret product.

questions.prompt: Which secret-handling design is appropriate for a Python service?
options: Put the secret in a prompt so the model can configure the service
Return it in a diagnostic response
Load it from an approved secret provider and redact it from errors, logs, traces, and exports
Store it in a source comment
questions.explanation: Secret access should be controlled and the value should not propagate into developer or operator channels unnecessarily.

review.note: Correct answer binds provider use to propagation controls.

questions.prompt: What does a dependency scanner finding establish by itself?
options: That compromise occurred
That the package is unreachable and harmless
That no update is needed
A triage signal requiring affected-path, reachability, ownership, and remediation analysis
questions.explanation: Scanner output informs a risk decision; it is neither proof of exploitation nor proof of safety.

review.note: Correctly limits scanner authority.

questions.prompt: Which build-provenance statement is correct?
options: A locked version alone proves the package source is trustworthy
A review should consider source, integrity, owner, build context, and CI credential exposure
A model-generated dependency is approved by default
Build tools have no security relevance
questions.explanation: Provenance is a set of assumptions and controls around source, integrity, ownership, execution context, and credentials; a lockfile is useful but not conclusive.

review.note: Supply-chain framing remains developer-specific and not exam-derived.

questions.prompt: Which acceptance criterion belongs in a Vibe Coding prompt for a secure endpoint?
options: Do not explain assumptions
Return code even if tests fail
Use the most complex framework available
State trust boundaries, allowed behavior, negative tests, and a human review checkpoint
questions.explanation: The prompt should make requirements and review observable. Complexity and unconditional generation are not security criteria.

review.note: Tests prompt requirements without assuming a product-specific workflow.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a vulnerable/secure/false-positive triad?
options: To provide exploit payloads for production
To make the model the final grader
To distinguish a confirmed weakness, an appropriate control, and a safe case whose assumptions must be checked
To replace all code review with pattern matching
questions.explanation: Triads train discrimination: the reviewer must recognize a real flow, a control, and a superficially similar but safe case without overclaiming.

review.note: Triad purpose is concrete and bounded to SPEC_ONLY teaching fixtures.

questions.prompt: After an AI repair appears to fix a finding, what is the next required step?
options: Delete the original requirement
Accept the diff because it is shorter
Publish it immediately
Run targeted positive, negative, and regression tests, then have a human verify the behavior and residual risk
questions.explanation: A repair can introduce semantic drift or a new weakness. Testing and independent human re-verification preserve the authority boundary.

review.note: Correctly preserves the full learning loop.

questions.prompt: What does a SPEC_READY_NON_EXECUTABLE capstone status mean?
options: The curriculum has a reviewed scenario and acceptance design, but no executable fixture or deployed lab has been claimed
A production lab is already deployed
The capstone is registered in runtime
All Evidence and Skill State records exist
questions.explanation: The status describes a content specification only. Future executable fixtures, harness evidence, and runtime work require separate gates and are not performed here.

review.note: Status meaning is explicit and avoids overclaiming implementation.
